canberra.title: Nearly 600 ACT public housing homes sit vacant. Why?
canberra.snippet: With affordable housing becoming one of Canberra’s biggest challenges, Budget Estimates has revealed 588 ACT public housing homes w...
canberra.content:
The ACT Government has built more public housing, but hundreds of properties still need upgrades. Photo: ACT Government.

With affordable housing becoming one of Canberra’s biggest challenges, Budget Estimates has revealed 588 ACT public housing homes were sitting vacant at the end of June — including 188 homes ready to be allocated to new tenants.

The figures sparked scrutiny during Thursday’s hearings, with independent MLA Thomas Emerson pressing Housing ACT officials over why so many homes were empty and whether the Territory’s ageing public housing stock was slowing the system down.

Housing ACT revealed the vacant properties included 285 undergoing repairs or upgrades, 57 awaiting decisions about their future, 43 earmarked for sale or redevelopment and 15 newly completed homes awaiting final handover.

With Housing Minister Suzanne Orr only days into the portfolio following last week’s Cabinet reshuffle, most of the questioning was directed at executive group manager, housing assistance Penny Shields and other senior Housing ACT officials.

The hearing quickly turned to a question many Canberrans would ask: if hundreds of public housing homes are empty, why aren’t more families moving in?

Housing ACT insisted the higher vacancy figure did not mean homes were sitting idle.

Instead, officials said the increase reflected properties moving through the repair process before being re-let.

Between the end of March and the end of June, 24 additional homes became vacant, while 89 homes completed repairs and became available for allocation.

“It just points to the amount of churn that we have through the portfolio, but also how quickly we’re getting those back maintained or upgraded … and then available for allocation,” executive branch manager, housing and inclusive policy Brooke Yates told the committee.

Mr Emerson then asked what many people waiting for housing would also want to know — how long do homes stay vacant before someone can move in?

Housing ACT could not provide an answer during the hearing, saying the timeframe depended on the work required and that average vacancy periods would be provided later.

The questioning also exposed the scale of the maintenance challenge facing the Territory’s public housing.

The opposition cited Productivity Commission data showing almost one in three Housing ACT homes are below an acceptable standard — the second-highest proportion in Australia.

Housing ACT acknowledged it was managing an ageing portfolio but said additional funding through last year’s Budget Review had allowed it to step up repairs and upgrades.

Officials said about 860 upgrade works were completed during the past financial year, helping more homes return to a condition where they could be leased again.

They acknowledged, however, that while the work made more existing homes available, it did not increase the overall number of public housing properties.

The hearing also heard Infrastructure Canberra is considering an offer from builders, tradespeople and suppliers to repair 20 vacant public housing homes before Christmas using pro bono labour.

Officials confirmed they had met with the group behind the proposal and agreed there was “a lot of merit” in the idea, although legal and property issues still needed to be worked through before it could proceed.

The discussion then broadened to the future of public housing in the ACT.

Budget Estimates heard public housing now makes up 5.48 per cent of all housing in the Territory, down from 7.6 per cent a decade ago. Officials said the Government remained committed to growing the portfolio to 13,200 homes by 2030, although they acknowledged further funding decisions would be needed to reach that target.

canberra.title: Regulator takes Optus to court over 000 outage
canberra.snippet: The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) has taken Optus to court over last year’s Triple Zero outage that adversely affe...
canberra.content:
The Australian Communications and Media Authority alleges Optus breached its legal obligations 1005 times in September last year. Photo: Optus.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) has taken Optus to court over last year’s Triple Zero outage that adversely affected people’s ability to connect to the emergency call service.

Two deaths were linked to the 18 September outage across parts of NSW, South Australia, Western Australia and the Northern Territory.

The service was offline for 13 hours, resulting in more than 600 calls failing to connect.

ACMA alleges that during the outage, Optus Mobile breached two separate legal obligations on 1005 occasions.

It says Optus failed to give end-users who made emergency calls using an emergency telephone service supplied by Optus Mobile access to the emergency call service.

And, ACMA alleges, it failed to ensure that those emergency calls were carried to the relevant termination point.

ACMA chair Nerida O’Loughlin said that providing access to the emergency call service is essential to protecting the Australian public.

“Australians rightly expect that when they call Triple Zero, their call will connect,” she said.

“The circumstances of this outage meant that did not reliably occur, leaving people unable to connect to potentially life-saving services.

“Giving access to the emergency call service is not optional, it is a fundamental legal obligation and the most important public safety responsibility telecommunications providers have.”

The proceedings follow earlier enforcement action taken by the ACMA arising from the Optus November 2023 outage.

Singtel Optus subsidiaries, including Optus Mobile, paid more than $12 million in infringement notice penalties imposed by the ACMA for breaches relating to emergency calls.

These included failures to give access to the emergency call service during that outage.

“The recurrence of a major network outage affecting emergency calls so soon after the November 2023 outage is a significant concern and one of the reasons the ACMA has decided to take this matter to court,” Ms O’Loughlin said.

“The ACMA will not hesitate to take strong enforcement action where alleged telco failures have jeopardised public access to the critical emergency call service.”

ACMA is seeking from the court declarations that Optus contravened the Telecommunications Act on the number of occasions the regulator claims, and an order that Optus Mobile pay pecuniary penalties to the Commonwealth for these contraventions.

The maximum penalty available to the court is $250,000 per contravention.

Communications Minister Anika Wells welcomed the independent regulator’s action.

“These are serious alleged failures by Optus,” the minister said.

“Australians rightly expect to reach Triple Zero when they need it most, and telcos are legally obligated to ensure that connection occurs.”

Optus has acknowledged the court action but says it is inappropriate to comment on the legal proceedings.

The telco has also issued a statement saying its focus remains on building a better Optus, continuing to invest in “network resilience,” and strengthening its systems.

Acting shadow communications minister Dan Tehan said every Australian should have the confidence they can call Triple Zero in times of emergency.

“Anything less is untenable,” he said.

“Action from the regulator should not have taken more than 10 months. The alleged failures by Optus, which led to several deaths, are extremely serious.

“On Minister Wells’ watch, Australians have endured repeated telecommunications failures with no urgency from the Albanese government.”

Telstra had a massive network outage early in July this year that also shut down access to Triple Zero around much of the country.

As with the Optus network failures, Telstra’s executives have appeared before a Senate inquiry.

The Federal Government promised a full investigation into the Telstra outages, suggesting ACMA might also determine if any penalty should be applied.

canberra.title: Greens call for moratorium on AI data centres
canberra.snippet: The Greens have called for an immediate moratorium on new artificial intelligence data centre approvals until the Federal Government gets...
canberra.content:
Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young says while states and territories argue with the Federal Government over AI, the tech giants continue to exploit Australian resources. Photo: Region.

The Greens have called for an immediate moratorium on new artificial intelligence data centre approvals until the Federal Government gets its rules sorted and Federal Parliament scrutinises the legislation.

AI is fast becoming the hottest political topic in Australia, with Queensland and the Northern Territory opposing much of Labor’s proposed national framework for the further rollout of the industry, and the federal Opposition suggesting nuclear energy should be included in the energy mix for data centres.

There are currently about 160 AI data centres operational across the country, but Anthony Albanese has flagged his government’s intention to encourage more tech giants to invest further in Australia.

The Prime Minister added, however, that strict standards and mandatory rules would be developed to ensure new AI data centres put more energy back into the grid than they use, embrace renewable energy, protect water supplies, provide local job opportunities, and don’t rip off the work of Australian authors, musicians and artists.

He is setting up the Office of AI within his own department, the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet.

But Greens communications spokesperson Sarah Hanson-Young said that’s all well and good, but Australian jurisdictions can’t get on the same page, so the brakes need to be applied.

She said the growing split between states showed that tech giants are already exploiting governments’ desperation to attract investment.

“Big AI is sitting back and laughing as governments fall over themselves in a race to the bottom to accommodate its every whim,” Senator Hanson-Young said.

“Queensland and the Northern Territory have both failed to get behind a national approach to ensuring data centres are powered by new renewable energy.

“Australia must present a united front in the face of this new extractive industry.

“Big AI is already looking for weaknesses it can exploit and playing governments off against each other.”

Senator Hanson-Young warned against allowing AI to become “another mining boom” where governments compete to give away Australian resources on the cheapest possible terms.

She said that, while parliament establishes national rules for data centres and AI, a moratorium had become necessary.

“We should not be rubber-stamping massive new data centres while parliament is still working out how to regulate the AI industry,” the Greens senator said.

“Australia must set the rules of engagement with Big AI, not the other way around.

“If we don’t get this right, we risk handing over our energy, water, land and natural environment to some of the world’s biggest corporations without getting a fair deal in return.

“Data centres must be powered by genuinely additional renewable energy and must not become a backdoor for new fossil fuel extraction.

“We cannot allow the AI boom to become an excuse for more gas, more pressure on our electricity grid and more destruction of Australia’s precious environment.

“We have seen what happens when governments let powerful corporations write the rules. This time, we need to put people and the environment first.

“Big AI can wait. Australia’s environment and communities can’t.”

The nation’s energy ministers met virtually on Tuesday (28 July), resulting in both Queensland and the NT pushing back against the Federal Government’s intention to legislate that large-scale data centres must underwrite new renewable power supply.

Queensland Energy Minister David Janetzki said his state would always support proposals that deliver affordable, reliable and sustainable power.

“However, we will not support underdeveloped ideas that hand increased power to Canberra at the expense of Queenslanders,” he said.

NT Energy Minister Gerard Maley said the Territory wanted to ensure that costs associated with data centre electricity demand were not passed on to consumers.

“While we will continue to engage in national discussions, any reforms must recognise the Territory’s unique electricity system and investment environment, rather than impose a one-size-fits-all approach,” he said.

National Cabinet meets in August to discuss progressing with national standards, with the PM hoping to reach agreement with all state and territory leaders on the issue.

Meanwhile, the Coalition has been talking up the potential for nuclear energy to power new AI data centres in Australia.

Shadow energy minister Dan Tehan has pointed to tech giants Google and Amazon investing in nuclear energy options in the United States and said the same should be considered in Australia.

Deputy Nationals leader Darren Chester has suggested it is inevitable that future data centres in Australia will be powered by nuclear energy to some degree.

Labor remains opposed to lifting the moratorium on nuclear energy in Australia.

canberra.title: Half-baked energy supply leaves local business’s expansion plans in the cold
canberra.snippet: Some Canberra hospitality businesses are finding themselves disadvantaged by renewable energy policies. Evoke Bakery is an award-winning ...
canberra.content:
30 July 2026

Join the conversation

8

Tom Lambert, Man Hoi ‘Kenny’ Cheng and Jayson Brockman run the award-winning Evoke Bakery. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Some Canberra hospitality businesses are finding themselves disadvantaged by renewable energy policies.

Evoke Bakery is an award-winning local business which opened in Curtin in 2022. They have since expanded to sites at Spence and Kippax shops.

Owner Tom Lambert told Region that he was looking at opening a new location in Dickson at the site formerly occupied by Commonwealth Bank, which has sat empty for a long time. They were very close to signing the lease when they hit a major snag: the ban on new gas connections meant that all equipment would need to be electric, but the site wouldn’t support a powerful enough connection.

“Bakeries need more power than most businesses for their ovens, provers, sheeters, mixers, fridges and even the coffee machine,” he said.

“They didn’t have enough power supply available [at this site]… We tried to find alternatives and spoke to EvoEnergy but we didn’t have any rights because we hadn’t signed a lease yet. It took months, but eventually we just decided not to go through with it.”

Evoenergy states that the wait time for new connections is currently over 12 months.

They’re not alone in having issues with having sufficient power supply to electrify their business.

Other restaurateurs have had electric equipment in storage for years while waiting for energy upgrades that would allow them to actually use it.

Tom Lambert said he is supportive of sustainable policies and keen to comply with the government push towards fully electric kitchens.

“It just shows that there’s a disconnect between those making the policy decisions and what’s actually happening,” said Tom.

An ACT Government spokesperson told Region: “The ACT Government is working closely with industry, consumers and network operators to support the transition to an increasingly electrified economy in a growing city.

“Electricity demand associated with the gas transition is one of a number of factors considered in network planning, but it is not expected to be the primary driver of future network investment.”

When asked about wait times for new connections, the spokesperson said the ACT Government is aware of concerns and considering regulatory reform.

In the case of Dickson Shops, the precinct currently has a number of empty shopfronts and works are underway through the City Renewal Authority’s Dickson Shops upgrade project.

“The upgrades will improve the public environment, creating a safer, more connected and inviting shopping and community hub while preserving the character of Dickson Shops. This will have a significant impact on the attractiveness of Dickson Shops to prospective tenants.”

Greens climate change spokesperson Andrew Braddock said it is clear that Labor and Evoenergy aren’t treating the net zero transition as a priority.

“The need for the electrical grid strengthening to support the electrification of gas and transport was absolutely considered in creating net zero and no new gas policies. The Greens, however, have been concerned the ACT Labor Government and Evoenergy have failed to prepare the grid for this predictable increase in load. This seriously compromises our net zero goals – and it’s clear Canberrans want us to get to net zero,” he said.

“It’s very disappointing to see a business getting locked out of the net zero transition.”

“We hope to see some action in the new Climate Change Strategy – but that is already delayed and overdue.”

In the meantime, Dickson has missed out on a new bakery and a local business has wasted time, money and energy on a dead end.

“We really wanted to move into Dickson and we just can’t,” Tom said.

“There’s nothing we can do about it.”

australia.title: Book returned to Australian library – 150 years overdue
australia.snippet: The book, Antiquities of Athens, was handed back to Kiama library by a man who found it bricked into a wall An Australian public library ...
australia.content:
An Australian public library has had a book returned an estimated 150 years late after being found behind a wall during a home renovation.

The book, Antiquities of Athens, published in 1858, was returned to the library in the seaside town of Kiama, south of Sydney, by a man who had found it inside a tea crate bricked into a sealed fireplace

“We’ve never had anything that old come back to us,” library manager Michelle Hudson said.

“I follow lots of libraries on social media and often you’ll get things that are maybe 30 or 40 years old when they’re cleaning out estates and stuff like that.”

The book’s finder did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The late return fine would be around A$28,000 (US$19,500), allowing for inflation, Hudson said. That was calculated on the British three pence a week overdue fee that was printed on the inside cover of the book, along with a list of rules that applied when the library opened in 1872.

But Hudson said there was no way of tracing the final borrower who had accrued the debt. The library journal from the 1870s that recorded who borrowed a book and when had been lost.

“Unfortunately, we have a missing link. There’s nothing in the book that tells us who the last borrower was,” Hudson said.

Library rules in the 1870s stated that a book had to be returned and an overdue debt paid before another book could be borrowed.

“Maybe that’s why they never returned it to us,” Hudson said.

Under the antiquated rules of the day, up to three books could be borrowed by households in which at least six members were “known to be able to read”.

The book, which has some water damage from its years under a chimney, was marked as No 506 in the library’s original collection of around 1,000 books, Hudson said.

She expects the book was lost within a few years of the library opening.

The returned book will be displayed in the library’s local history collection.

“We’re not going to allow it to go back out again. We don’t want to wait another 150 years for this book to be returned,” Hudson said.

australia.title: Kumanjayi Little Baby murder trial delayed until December – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Minister says meeting Closing the Gap target a major...
australia.content:
Kumanjayi Little Baby murder case delayed over ‘significant volume’ of forensic evidence

The court process following the alleged murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby will be delayed for months, due to a “significant volume” of forensic evidence that had yet to be processed.

The five-year-old Warlpiri girl was found dead in April after a five-day search following her sudden disappearance from an Alice Springs town camp. A 47-year-old man, Jefferson Lewis, was later charged with murder.

On Thursday, the Alice Springs local court heard there was a “significant volume” of evidence that had not yet been fully examined or collected as part of the investigation, including 100 different forensic requests and 20 outstanding police witness statements.

The court heard a “very substantial brief” of evidence had already been served in the matter, including 76 statements from different witnesses, 48 pieces of police body-worn footage, drone footage, CCTV footage, and a preliminary postmortem report. A full autopsy report was expected to be handed over in the near future.

The matter returns to court on 3 December.

– Samantha Jonscher in Alice Springs

What we learned, Thursday 30 July

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for today.

Before we go, here’s a recap of the day’s top headlines:

  • The special envoy to combat antisemitism made another appearance in the royal commission’s hot seat today.

  • One of the 19 Closing the Gap targets has officially been reached after early childhood education enrolment for First Nations children hit 95% across the country.

  • The government announced the second stage of its mandatory safety training for childcare workers will begin Friday, focused on preventing child safety concerns and detecting grooming.

  • Victoria pushed for a national crackdown on hidden ticketing fees and deceptive dynamic pricing practices when Australian consumer affairs state ministers met with the commonwealth’s assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and Treasury, Andrew Leigh, in Darwin today.

  • The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, has taken messaging service Telegram to court over its alleged failure to detect and remove pro-terror material from its platform, including videos of terrorist executions and mass shootings.

  • Luke Gosling, the federal member for Solomon, was arrested this morning over an alleged assault earlier this month, Northern Territory police said in a statement.

  • The Australian Communications and Media Authority has taken Optus to court over the September 2025 triple-zero outage.

  • The number of suspected deadly bird flu cases continues to grow in South Australia, with 13 more in greater crested terns, the state government said. Victoria has also confirmed its first case of the disease in a greater crested tern – a common local seabird – found at Portland.

  • Neil the seal has racked up a bill of more than $36,000 for his most-recent stay in Tasmania.

  • The drugmaker AstraZeneca will continue to provide women with breast cancer and endometriosis free access to the vital medicine Zoladex, which the company said last month would be removed from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.

  • The court process following the alleged murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby will be delayed for months, due to a “significant volume” of forensic evidence that had yet to be processed.

Teacher wearing ‘Free Palestine’ badge made student feel ‘very unsafe in the classroom’, royal commission told

Following on from our previous post:

The first witness to front the royal commission on Thursday was a mother sharing her son’s experience with antisemitism at school.

She said the school made efforts to ensure the safety of her son and spoke to the offending students.

But she said education needed to apply to teachers as well, referring to one occasion where her son removed himself from a classroom when a teacher wore a “Free Palestine” badge featuring a fist of resistance.

“Words and symbols can mean different things to different people and, to him, that badge made him feel very unsafe in the classroom,” the mother said.

“Even a badge promoting peace between Israel or Palestine, from my perspective, shouldn’t be worn into a classroom. It’s not the place for it.”

– AAP

James Patterson says the Coalition is open to working with One Nation on proposed terror plans

The shadow minister for defence, James Paterson, says the Coalition is “willing to work” with One Nation on plans to introduce new laws to block the return of Australian citizens with links to terror groups, including Islamic State.

Pauline Hanson has appealed to the Coalition, which rebuffed her, and told media outlets on Thursday she would seek to introduce her own legislation to make it easier to cancel passports and block returns.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Paterson said:

We are willing to work with anyone who wants to stop these Isis fighters coming to Australia, and Tony Burke’s answer … gives me no comfort and should give the Australian people no comfort that this government is doing everything they can to protect us from someone who left our country to join one of the most reprehensible terrorist organisations the planet has ever seen.

Antisemitism at schools underreported because students believe ‘nothing would happen’, royal commission hears

Students at Australia’s largest Jewish day school have given up reporting incidents of antisemitism due to their frequency and the lack of consequences for perpetrators, the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion has heard, as reported by AAP.

John Hamey was head of Sydney’s Moriah College from 2011 until 2018 and appeared at the royal commission earlier today.

He shared frequent incidents of Jewish students being targeted by pupils from other schools and members of the public. Hamey told the inquiry:

There were often taunts that invoked the gas chamber and statements along the lines of ‘Hitler should have finished the job’.

Students were being worn down by frequent traumatic incidents, which got brushed off as “just something that they had to deal with and they had to get on with”, the former principal said:

It was not necessarily something they would report because they would say, ‘well, nothing would happen’, or there’d be no serious outcome or consequence for the perpetrators of that antisemitism.

Hamey said most teachers outside Jewish institutions were not well informed about Jewish cultural life or equipped to identify antisemitism. He said:

They really lack the language.

Because it’s too politically contentious, they will minimise those actions and just deal with them as … one-off incidences or just a simple form of bullying.

ACTU backs royal commission into Victoria’s construction sector￼

The outgoing ACTU national secretary, Sally McManus, has cautiously welcomed a royal commission into Victoria’s construction sector, saying the union movement has long believed there needed to be “way more done to completely rid that sector of organised crime”.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, McManus said:

The union movement is allergic to royal commissions because we have been through three or four and seen them as just focusing on workers and the unions and used in that way.

However, in the case of Victoria it is very clear there is a whole ecosystem of criminality. I think it is both organised crime and probably disorganised crime.

I don’t think there is any one person who could say this is perfectly what this ecosystem looks like and that any royal commission needs to focus on all of it.

‘Not good enough’: pleas to act on Closing the Gap targets

Authorities are being urged to work more closely with Indigenous groups as Closing the Gap targets fall badly behind expectations, AAP reports.

Out of 19 targets towards the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, five areas are improving but are not on track to be met and four are worsening. Just three areas targeting socioeconomic disparity are likely to be met on time, a Productivity Commission report found.

First Nations preschool enrolments are the sole target being met nationally, more than halfway through the 2031 agreement period.

Achieving that milestone was important, Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy told ABC RN on Thursday. She said.

That is because of the work of the Aboriginal and community-controlled sector and those involved in the preschool sector.

But it was clear “challenges remain” in addressing all other targets, including ones to do with incarceration rates.

The outlook is so bleak national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children Sue-Anne Hunter warned officials should be stood down for the lack of progress. She told the ABC.

If this was any other national agreement that was going backwards or just staying still, someone would actually lose their job.

We can’t have an agreement that we’re not adhering to ... it’s not good enough.

Coalition of Peaks lead convener, Donnella Mills, added her voice to the growing concern, saying federal, state and territory governments needed to work more collaboratively with Indigenous groups. She said:

Governments need to do more to embed the priority reforms in their work to close the gap and achieve the outcomes our people have fought for over decades, especially those governments where targets are going backwards or have stalled.

Penry Buckley

Dominic Perrottet’s brother allegedly said he paid for new Liberal party memberships, Icac hears

Reformers member Robert Assaf is giving evidence again, as NSW Icac hearings resume after a break for lunch.

This morning, the commission heard from Assaf that despite an agreement between the Reformers that they would not pay for the memberships of new members they were signing up in alleged branch-stacking efforts, he had “suspicions from conversations” that some people working with the Reformers were in fact paying for memberships.

Under Liberal party rules, if a person discloses that their membership had been paid for, their local branch could be frozen. Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, resumes this line of questioning about which prominent Reformers he was concerned were paying for membership, but Assaf says:

They didn’t like didn’t confess it to me, but I got enough of a rumour. I had to tell them be careful in case that is happening.

Dwyer reads to Assaf from an interview he gave to Icac before public hearings in which he claimed that Jean-Claude Perrottet, younger brother of former Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, had paid for memberships in the Hills Shire.

Dwyer: “You told the commission, didn’t you, that Jean-Claude Perrottet told you that he had to pay or that he would pay for memberships because he was relying on a lot of his friends doing it, and there needed to be some incentive?”

Assaf: “Correct.”

Today, Assaf says he never witnessed Jean-Claude Perrottet paying for memberships, but understands that he would reimburse the cost of signing up or buy a new member dinner to cover the cost. Jean-Claude Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Two Jacinta Allan supporters to quit politics

Benita Kolovos

Victorian government ministers Lily D’Ambrosio and Harriet Shing have announced they will step down from cabinet and quit politics at the election.

The duo are among the closest supporters of Jacinta Allan, who resigned as premier on Tuesday before a leadership spill brought on by Ben Carroll.

In a statement this afternoon, Carroll said both D’Ambrosio and Shing have “brought compassion, determination and a strong sense of purpose to their roles, delivering outcomes that have improved the lives of Victorians and strengthened the communities they represent”.

D’Ambrosio has been the MP for Mill Park for 24 years and is the longest-serving energy minister in Australia. She said:

Back in 2014 not a lot of people thought about energy too much. Of course, the decade that followed changed all that. Under Labor, Victoria has led the nation, paving the way for Australia’s transition to renewable energy. Where Victoria has gone, the rest of country has followed.

Shing was recently promoted to health minister. She has also previously served as minister for equality, housing, the Suburban Rail Loop and water. She told Carroll of her plans to step down on Tuesday afternoon, after his elevation to premier. Shing said:

This chapter has been the honour of my life. I have worked hard, with and for the communities and people I have represented. And it has been a labour of love and determination.

Carroll said the Labor caucus will meet on Monday morning to elevate new ministers and then he will announce his cabinet “shortly following”. Expect a lot of jostling by MPs and their respective factions over the weekend.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take things from here. Enjoy your arvo!

Petra Stock

Extra precautions for threatened species at Zoos Victoria

Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, has said the state government has been working with Zoos Victoria over the past two years to improve biosecurity measures in response to H5 bird flu for threatened species held at Victorian facilities, including captive insurance populations of helmeted honeyeater, orange-bellied parrot, plains wanderer and regent honeyeater.

He said:

Zoos Victoria has been doing a range of work around increasing the biosecurity of the facilities that hold those species, so they’re not at risk from visits from either wild birds or the public, but also enhancing biosecurity processes and arrangements to adequately protect those captive populations.

Otherwise, he said, there had been no change to zoo operations in Victoria.

Since the arrival of H5 bird flu in Australia, Perth zoo has installed precautions including additional barriers, hand sanitizer stations and signage, while Adelaide zoo has temporarily closed its walk-through aviaries and suspended its bird show.

Patrick Commins

Dwelling approvals rise, but not fast enough to meet target

Dwelling approvals jumped to more than 205,000 in 2025-26, reaching the highest level in five years but still well short of what’s needed to meet the government’s ambitious homebuilding target.

The latest figures from the ABS showed 17,305 more approvals in the last financial year versus the previous, an increase of 9%.

House approvals were at their highest since 2021-22, and approvals to build non-house dwellings (apartments and townhouses and so forth) were at the highest since 2017-18, the ABS said.

Labor has set a target of 1.2m homes being built over five financial years to mid-2029, but few expect it to be achieved.

Master Builders Australia said there needed to be 253,000 approvals in 2025-26 to catch up to the Housing Accord target, and that the industry was being held back by high costs, low productivity and a shortage of workers.

The National Housing Supply and Affordability Council estimates the 1.2m new homes target will be met by September 2030 – so about 15 months late.

Denita Wawn, Master Builders CEO, noted that building a home costs 50% more now than it did before the pandemic. This year’s global oil crisis has also sent the price of some building materials soaring.

A Productivity Commission interim report this week found that regulation has become “a handbrake” on new housing supply. Among the PC’s interim recommendations was sweeping land-use reform to allow higher density dwellings in our cities.

Petra Stock

Public reports to Victorian bird flu hotline go from 10 a week to more than 100 a day

Continuing the update on Victoria’s first H5N1 detection, the state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said bird flu reports from members of the public had gone from about 10 a week to “well over 100 some days”, with about 10% being tested.

He said there was now “clear evidence of transmission” in South Australia, with the disease moving from one bird to another.

Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said:

We know from elsewhere in the world that if the virus were to be established in Victoria, then – particularly in wildlife – there’d be little we could do to actually minimise the spread or the impact on wildlife. If it were to establish, our focus would be on surveillance, ensuring public safety, ensuring communications with the public, but also looking to protect at-risk species where that’s possible.

“Establishment” means the disease has taken hold. But Cooke said that threshold required more evidence of the disease spreading between multiple types of birds and native species, and evidence of the disease mixing and changing within native populations.

On Wednesday, a national group of federal, state and territory officials enacted a national agreement for responding to H5 bird flu incursions, based on advice that: “H5 bird flu in wildlife is not technically feasible to eradicate following recent detections and evidence of local transmission of H5 bird flu in a small number of wild seabirds”.

Members of the public are urged to avoid contact with any dead or sick birds or animals showing signs of bird flu. Report sightings to the emergency animal disease hotline 1800 675 888 or birdflu.gov.au.

Tom McIlroy

Labor unimpressed with Hanson’s terror plan

The federal government has dismissed Pauline Hanson’s plans to introduce new laws to block the return of Australian citizens with links to terror groups including Islamic State.

After the One Nation leader’s appeal to work with the Coalition on the plans to block people found to have worked with or assisted terror groups was rebuffed, Hanson told media outlets on Thursday she would seek to introduce her own legislation that would make it easier to cancel passports and block returns.

But the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, is less than impressed.

He said Labor was using laws introduced by the former Coalition government, describing them as going “right to the limit of what you could do constitutionally”.

“Every Australian, me included, doesn’t want these individuals back,” Burke said in Queensland.

You know, when people have made a decision to join something as horrific as that, you don’t want them back.

The reality is every country in the world has to take back its own citizens. And I would just say people should be very wary of letting go of the principle that countries have to take their citizens back.

Burke said it was in Australia’s national interest that countries took back their own citizens, even if they’re accused of terror offences overseas.

Anyone who wants to depart from that principle needs to explain why they think it would be OK for the 750 people every year who I make leave, for them to have to stay here because I don’t think Australians would cop it.

australia.title: ‘Warring kingdoms’: cofounder of religious Reformers compares NSW Liberal party factionalism to Braveheart
australia.snippet: Robert Assaf tells Icac that Angus Taylor wasn’t ‘that involved’ but the federal opposition leader ‘definitely wasn’t opposed’ to work of...
australia.content:
A member of a group of young conservative Liberal power brokers being investigated for allegedly soliciting illegal donations has compared their factional work to Mel Gibson’s Braveheart – and said they “didn’t think the law applied to us” when it came to political funding.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday heard from Robert Assaf, the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.

Icac is investigating whether Liberal figures, including Assaf, “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch-stacking”. The Reformers allegedly wanted more conservative policies on issues including same-sex marriage, transgender rights, abortion and euthanasia.

Assaf, 30, who admitted to being one of two founding members of the Reformers in 2017, said the group was started in the context of a factional split in the Liberal party between the religious conservative hard right and the centre-right.

“My observations at the time were, the right faction was like – I’m not sure if you’ve seen Braveheart – but like these warring kingdoms, and they would slaughter each other, and then every now and then they’d come together for a big fight,” Assaf said.

While branch-stacking is not of itself illegal, Icac is investigating whether the alleged conduct of the Reformers involved possible offences under NSW’s Electoral Funding Act. Asked about his knowledge of the laws governing donations, Assaf told Icac that the group “didn’t think the law applied to us”.

“Because it was an electoral law, we’re not campaigning in elections in that sense,” he told counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC.

“We’re internal Liberal party machinations. My understanding the whole way through was, until very recently … was it’s internal. It doesn’t count as anything to do with electoral laws or any other law.”

He defended the Reformers, which includes members being investigated over a second allegation: that they took $2m in payments from the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for outcomes sought by Nassif.

“The Reformers sound really spooky in the media right now, but it was just a bunch of 20-year-old people trying to figure things out,” Assaf said.

Assaf appeared after two days of evidence from former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, who was associated with the group but has not been named in allegations against the Reformers.

After being mentioned during Whitelaw’s examination on Tuesday and Wednesday, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, dodged further questions on Thursday after denying he had ever donated to the Reformers.

“I’ve answered these questions yesterday. I’m not going to give a running commentary on it,” Taylor said. The federal Liberal leader is not accused of wrongdoing.

On Thursday, Assaf claimed Taylor was one of several state and federal Liberal politicians who were aware of and supported the Reformers’ work.

“Angus was around it, but I don’t think he was really that involved,” Assaf said. “He definitely wasn’t opposed.”

He said the former NSW Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, whose brothers Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet are named in the Icac allegations, was “pretty absent in the whole thing, but supportive from what I understood”. Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.

The commission heard Assaf went to the same independent Catholic schoolas Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet, as well as another member of the Reformers, Jeremy Greenwood.

After spending a year in a Catholic seminary, Assaf later worked in federal parliament for various ministers, senators and MPs, including Tony Abbott, who the commission heard gave talks at recruitment events hosted by the Reformers.

He described having an “icky feeling” about getting involved in politics, but said he was convinced to join the Liberal party after attending a 2015 talk at the Sydney University Liberal club by NSW upper house member Damien Tudehope, against the Safe Schools program, whose stated aim was to keep gay and transgender students safe.

Assaf, who described Tudehope as “a warrior for the values that he cared about”, said the politician subsequently gave numerous talks at events hosted by the Reformers.

Tudehope, who is not accused of wrongdoing, stepped aside from his role as shadow attorney general and Liberal upper house leader after being called as a witness by Icac.

The inquiry heard that Assaf and fellow Reformer, Christian Ellis, started the group in 2017, after forming a strong friendship while working together on the No campaign for the same-sex marriage plebiscite.

The inquiry heard that adopting the model that had seen Assaf recruited, the group began to organise talks on conservative issues, aiming to sign up new members afterwards.

Dwyer on Thursday showed Assaf a draft document sent to him by Ellis which detailed a plan to recruit 5,000 Christian conservative members to the party to take control of the NSW division of the Liberal party, which had 4,000 members at the time.

Assaf said the main aim of the Reformers was “policy change” but increasing the number of members in the Liberal party was “certainly part of the process”.

Asked about a stated aim “to take over left-wing branches through stealth”, Assaf said “ideally, we would not want to take branches through stealth”.

“I prefer to be a front stabber than a back stabber,” he added, stating the group’s intention was to create a “broad church” within the party. Assaf said they wanted to “change the terrible situation of factionalism”.

“Christians obviously don’t like lying,” he said. “But there was a strategy to it, and some people needed to be more comfortable with that than others.”

The inquiry heard the Reformers expanded to include members such as Jean-Claude Perrottet and Greenwood and began to have success taking over branches.

“Great news. God’s granted us a victory. We’ve officially taken the Coffs Harbor branch away from the left wing,” wrote Assaf in one email.

But the inquiry heard Assaf became concerned that some Reformers were paying for the cost of new memberships, a practice which under Liberal party rules would see branches frozen.

Under questioning from Dwyer, Assaf said this included Jean-Claude Perrottet, while his brother Dominic Perrottet was serving as a NSW MP.

“Anything [Jean-]Claude did at that time, noting his brother’s position, I was sensitive to,” he said. Jean-Claude Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Assaf occasionally clashed with Dwyer over his ability to remember details about the Reformers, including an agreement with prohibited donor Michael O’Hara.

On Monday, O’Hara admitted to a fake arrangement in which he paid registered lobbyist Beckington, founded by Christian Ellis, for “strategic wealth strategy investment advice” when in fact he understood he was paying to “get my conservative values into the Liberal Party”. But he disputed whether the payments to the Reformers were to the NSW Liberals or should be considered political donations.

At one point on Thursday, Dwyer asked Assaf, “Can I suggest to you that in fact you were aware of this arrangement, whether your memory is being refreshed or not?”

Assaf said: “You can suggest it, but the problem is … my memory is my memory.”

But Assaf, who admitted to the bogus arrangement with O’Hara, said the Reformers later became concerned that Ellis was “getting rich” on the money rather than using it for factional work. O’Hara told Ellis he would end the arrangement.

“Ellis might have to cancel the upgrade to his fifth Land Cruiser, ha ha ha ha,” Assaf wrote in a message to Greenwood and Jean-Claude Perrottet.

The inquiry heard that Assaf, Greenwood and Jean-Claude Perrottet were able to salvage the arrangement with O’Hara directing the money to another vehicle not controlled by Ellis. Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote in a message: ‘O’Hara saved”, to which Greenwood replied “Good work. How’s your mouth taste.”

“That sounds like a crass reference,” Assaf told the inquiry.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Fauci takes aim at News Corp journalist; Bikram Lama’s body returns home; and what to do about cultural collapse
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Dr Anthony Fauci, the pandemic-era US chief medical adviser, has described a book by News Corp investigative journalist Sharri Markson backing the “lab leak” theory of Covid-19’s origins as a “bunch of nonsense” in his newly released diaries.

This week, Fauci, 85, was subpoenaed by the Republican senator Rand Paul to appear at a Senate hearing on the origins of Covid-19, where he refused to answer questions, invoking the fifth amendment and accusing Paul of having an “unhinged obsession” with him.

Ahead of Fauci’s appearance, Paul published 1,141 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era journal entries, Caitlin Cassidy reports. In the entries, Fauci criticised reporting in The Australian newspaper and a book by Markson that claimed a facility in Wuhan was “immersed in genetically manipulating bat-coronaviruses in perilous experiments”.

Fauci, who served under seven US presidents but became a household name in 2020, wrote in his private diary that Markson’s reporting “does not make any sense”.

But Markson backed her work, saying she “led the way internationally exposing the role of Anthony Fauci’s agency funding 65 projects at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, funnelling the money through EcoHealth Alliance”.

Top news

  • ‘Warring kingdoms’: cofounder of religious Reformers compares NSW Liberal party factionalism to Braveheart

  • Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling charged with assaulting NT administrator

  • Ben Carroll will not rule out redirecting Suburban Rail Loop funds to other projects

  • Queensland MP pens ‘White Men Can Sprint’ social media post after Lachlan Kennedy takes silver in Glasgow

  • After eight months, Bikram Lama’s body is going home to Nepal. ‘My heart will finally find some peace,’ his mother says

  • Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 23 as aftershock and heat complicate rescue efforts

  • Gina Rinehart lobbied for controversial plan to move 2032 Olympic rowing to crocodile-inhabited river

In pictures

A deer walks through a smouldering forest after a wildfires near Saumos, in southwestern France.

France and Spain are on high alert as the fourth heatwave of the summer complicates ongoing efforts to tackle devastating wildfires in both countries.

What they said …

“I hope he is given the space and time he needs.” – Brendan Blomeley

The mayor of the Tasmanian council area where Neil the seal regularly visits has wished the elephant seal well after revealing his 15-day stay at Seven Mile beach cost the local Clarence city council a total of $31,540.53.

Podcast

Guardian Essential report: the Labor health check

This month’s Guardian Essential poll shows signs that One Nation’s primary vote continues to plateau. But Labor can’t breathe a big sigh of relief just yet.

Guardian Australia political reporter Josh Butler speaks with Guardian columnist and executive director of Essential, Peter Lewis, about the health of the government at the halfway point of Anthony Albanese’s second term as prime minister

Listen to the episode here.

Before bed read

In Sarah Wilson’s new book, one page is mostly blank. It’s intended as a reprieve, a neutral space “for you to stare at for a minute while your feelings catch up”.

You will need it. In I Eat the Stars, Wilson argues that the world as we know it is in collapse – and that we are too late to avoid the worst.

But the book also delivers clarity, writes Elle Hunt. Yes, things are that bad, but there is still plenty to fight for and much we can shape – if we are willing to confront reality.

Daily word game

Today’s starter word is: VERD. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.

Sign up

If you would like to receive this Afternoon Update to your email inbox every weekday, sign up here, or start your day with a curated breakdown of the key stories you need to know with our Morning Mail newsletter. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland.

australia.title: Archibald prize 2026: portrait of Jewish leader after Bondi terror attack wins people’s choice award
australia.snippet: Artist Michael Zavros says he was inspired by a deep respect for Alex Ryvchin’s leadership, as well as an uncanny likeness between the tw...
australia.content:
An artist’s portrayal of a Jewish leader produced just weeks after the Bondi massacre has won the Archibald people’s choice category.

Michael Zavros won the $5,000 prize for his portrait of Alex Ryvchin, the co-head of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, who Zavros called an “unmistakably and unashamedly Jewish” leader.

This year 45,769 votes were cast, the highest number ever received.

Zavros said he was inspired by a deep respect for Ryvchin’s leadership of the Jewish community, as well as an uncanny likeness between the two men.

  • Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

“A few years ago, my mother thought she saw me on TV, but it wasn’t, it was Alex,” Zavros said.

“As a natural leader, he spoke with clarity and conviction about the grief within his community and the changes he feared were emerging in our nation.”

The painting was created after the two men met in early January at a beach in Sydney’s east, just weeks after the Bondi terror attack. 

“I wanted to paint him in water, or the sea, which carries so much rich symbolism,” the artist said.

Also included was a tefillin, which is a small black leather box with leather straps that contains scrolls inscribed with verses from the Torah.

Zavros said the cultural symbols matter as they can express faith, history, and belonging, yet too often are used to divide and to harm.

It was so important to the artwork, the portrait was officially named Alex with his tefillin in the sea.

“It’s something that binds Jewish people to thousands of years of custom, it binds us to our almighty, and for me personally, binds me to someone who was very dear to me, someone who I lost at Bondi,” Ryvchin said. 

“Every time I would see him, without fail, we would do tefillin together and in the moments before he was killed … I’m sure at this moment he’s smiling at what he’s seeing.”

A couple of years ago, Zavros took a DNA test and unexpectedly discovered that he had Ashkenazi Jewish heritage, alongside his Greek and Irish ancestry, which is a new side to himself he is still learning about. 

“It’s worth reminding ourselves how fortunate we are to live in this great Western liberal democracy that welcomed my family from Cyprus in the 1950s, and welcomed Alex who arrived from the Ukraine as a four-year-old refugee in the 1980s,” he said.

The $100,000 Archibald prize was won by Richard Lewer for his portrait of artist Iluwanti Ken. The 105-year-old prize is awarded to the best portrait of a person “distinguished in art, letters, science or politics” painted by an Australian resident.

Self-taught artist Sean Layh’s portrait of actor Jacob Collins won him the $3,000 packing room prize, which is decided by the AGNSW staff who hang the paintings each year.

The Wynne prize for landscape painting and figurative sculpture, and the Sulman prize for genre, subject and mural painting are also awarded alongside the Archibald each year. This year the $50,000 Wynne prize went to Gaypalani Waṉambi for her painting The Waṉambi tree, while the $40,000 Sulman prize went to Lucy Culliton for Toolah, a painting of one of her seven greyhounds.

A record 2,524 entries were received across the Archibald, Wynne and Sulman prizes this year.

The Archibald, Wynne and Sulman Prizes 2026 exhibition is open at the Art Gallery of New South Wales until 16 August, before the Archibald finalists begin a regional tour across Victoria and New South Wales.

Australian Associated Press contributed to this report.

world.title: Record absence of world’s oldest head of state reignites health speculation
world.snippet: Cameroon’s president has not made statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June A record 53-day ...
world.content:
A record 53-day absence of the world’s oldest head of state has renewed speculation in his native Cameroon about whether he is dead or alive, even though discussing his health is illegal in the country.

On 7 June, 93-year-old Paul Biya departed for Switzerland for what officials described as a “brief private stay” alongside his wife, Chantal. Almost two months later, neither the president nor the first lady have addressed the country or been seen publicly.

Biya, who took office in 1982 after a seven-year stint as prime minister, has taken increasingly long absences from Cameroon in recent years, spending much of his time at the five-star InterContinental hotel in Geneva.

No official timetable has been announced for the president’s return from his latest trip abroad, leaving Cameroonians to rely on a succession of conflicting statements from government officials.

The minister of communication, René Emmanuel Sadi, said Biya was in good health and “working from Geneva, where he currently resides”.

“Reports claiming otherwise are pure fantasy and malicious manipulation aimed at destabilising opinion,” he added. Jacques Fame Ndongo, a senior official from the ruling party and the higher education minister, said Biya had been “meticulously following the files submitted to him by his aides … wherever he is”.

The labour minister, Grégoire Owona, gave a different explanation, saying the president was on annual leave and comparing him to regular Cameroonian citizens. “Paul Biya, elected by the Cameroonian people and paid by them, is a worker who has the right to annual leave,” he said. “His employer is obliged to grant it. He informed his employer before leaving and will do the same upon his return.”

Cameroonian authorities banned discussion of Biya’s health in October 2024, during another absence. Nevertheless, local media have published claims in recent weeks that he is critically ill, and jokes about Biya being a work-from-abroad president or a remote-work president, have resurfaced on social media.

Mamadou Mota, the vice-president of the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement party, said Biya’s latest absence had created a “glaring institutional vacuum”. “A country cannot be governed by remote control while critical socioeconomic challenges go unaddressed,” he said.

Last November, Biya was sworn in for his eighth consecutive seven-year term, a month after a presidential election marred by widespread allegations of irregularities and voter suppression. Although the Constitutional Council dismissed post-electoral complaints by opposition parties, many of them refused to recognise the outcome, arguing that the election had further eroded public confidence in Cameroon’s democratic institutions.

Biya has yet to name a government since being sworn in for his latest term. With parliamentary and municipal elections expected in early 2027, many are worried that the ripple effect of that and his prolonged absence could disrupt the electoral cycle.

Cameroon has the largest economy in central Africa, but unemployment rates, high inflation and poor public infrastructure are stymieing the prospects of its young people, who make up about two-thirds of its estimated population of 30.6 million.

“Politics should be about serving the people, but the [ruling] CPDM [party] appears more interested in holding on to power than addressing the concerns of Cameroonians,” said Kohtem Sambit, the secretary general of the opposition Movement for Patriotism and People’s Prosperity.

“The minister of the economy borrowed more than 21bn [Central African francs] in the name of the Cameroonian people, saying it was approved by Mr Biya,” Sambit told the Guardian. “How do we justify this? You do not see the person who signed, nor do you know his whereabouts. That debt will be paid by the public.”

Referring to Owona’s remarks, Sambit said: “If the president is on annual leave, he is still accountable to the Cameroonian people because he is paid with taxpayers’ money. His whereabouts should therefore be disclosed.”

Another opposition party, the Social Democratic Front, has argued that the issue is not whether the president has a constitutional right to travel, but rather the government’s failure to explain the extension of what had initially been described as a brief private visit. Another opposition leader, Patricia Tomaïno Ndam Njoya, of the Cameroon Democratic Union, has called for an impartial procedure to determine any “temporary or permanent incapacity of the head of state”.

In April, parliament reintroduced the office of vice-president as part of a constitutional overhaul, but the position has yet to be filled, leaving Cameroon without a designated deputy should the president become incapacitated. As Biya’s son and stepson reportedly jockey for position, public disagreements between cabinet ministers have become commonplace.

Last week, the party’s secretary general, Jean Nkuete, convened a rare meeting of senior party officials. The CPDM described the gathering only as an “important working session” and released neither an agenda nor further details. Attempts to obtain comment from senior party figures were unsuccessful. Several party officials have declined interview requests, citing personal reasons.

For the businessman Nji Lucas, the president’s prolonged absence has also become an economic concern. “I do not have confidence because it is almost as if the country is on autopilot,” he said. “No serious investor wants to commit resources in a country where there is uncertainty over political leadership. There is no trust, and investors require certainty before making long-term decisions.”

world.title: A quarter of young Africans believe USAID cuts could be positive, survey finds
world.snippet: Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influen...
world.content:
A quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US could have a positive impact, saying that losing foreign money will force leaders to confront and solve their own challenges, according to a new survey.

In Ghana and Nigeria, almost half (41% and 40% respectively) of young people aged 18 to 24 were optimistic, with Liberia not far behind (37%). A further one in 10 (11%) young people were uncertain about the impact, according to the African Youth Survey, which interviewed almost 5,000 people across 16 of the continent’s 54 recognised countries.

The Trump administration announced in early 2025 that it was eliminating more than 90% of USAID’s foreign contracts and $60bn in overall US assistance around the world. US foreign aid had been designed to play a critical role in tackling poverty, hunger and inequality worldwide.

Other countries, including Britain, France and Germany, have also been slashing aid budgets. The UK announced in February 2025 that the aid budget would be cut from 0.5% of gross national income to 0.3% in 2027, its lowest level as a percentage of national income since records began. The UN target is 0.7%.

Ivor Ichikowitz, whose South African family foundation commissioned the report, said: “The big picture [from the survey] is that the youth is concerned about governments that are overly influenced by foreign powers. What they’re saying is that African governments need to take agency and responsibility for their own reality.”

Africa has the youngest population in the world, with 70% of sub-Saharan Africa under the age of 30, according to the UN. The median age of the continent is 19 years and six months. By 2030, Africa will be home to more than 40% of the world’s youth.

The sudden USAID cuts were met with public outrage and pushback from development and humanitarian organisations. They caused the closure of vital services, including maternity clinics, and medicine shortages at a time when UN agencies are struggling to find money for their humanitarian work and food insecurity has been worsened by the climate crisis.

According to the survey, nearly half of African youth (46%) did believe the closure of USAID would have a damaging impact on their countries, with healthcare services and disease prevention seen as the areas most affected. This anxiety is highest in Mozambique (76%), followed by Kenya (63%) and Rwanda (63%), where youth feel the cuts will disproportionately affect the most vulnerable members of society.

Degan Ali, executive director of Adeso, an African non-profit incubating ideas and enterprises to lower aid dependency, said that while the cuts were carried out in a “hugely irresponsible and inhumane” manner, she was not surprised that a significant proportion of young people saw positivity there. “I think it’s a reflection of the general feeling. A lot of people find aid very demeaning,” she said. “They didn’t feel that the aid was being used for the right things and there is a sense of ‘We can do this for ourselves’. The younger generation feel like our leaders are the duty bearers and are supposed to be handling the needs of our communities.”

She said people believed that the aid that comes into a country is not going to the right causes or the right people. “There’s all this money going into the development sector, but they’re not really seeing major changes on the ground,” she said. “The younger generation is very politically active and more savvy. They are pushing back and trying to hold their leaders accountable.”

She also said that the youth was looking towards African role models on the continent, a move exemplified by the popularity of Burkina Faso’s military leader, Ibrahim Traoré, who portrays himself as a pan-Africanist figure leading his nation out of the clutches of western imperialism and neocolonialism.

“He is one of the more popular leaders across the entire continent of Africa,” said Ali. “There are matatus (minibus taxis) that have his name on in Nairobi, Kenya. The youth see that he is turning around a very poor country and that he really cares about his people. That further motivates young people to protest and say, ‘We don’t need aid, we have enough resources in our country and we need our leaders to behave differently.’”

Hibak Kalfan, executive director of Near, a network of civil society organisations from the global south, said the shuttering of USAID had led to the closure of initiatives and organisations across the whole continent, but had also created the opportunity to reconsider resources and sustainability. “It has put a real light on the fact that [organisations] have been highly dependent on bilateral external funding for years, and the future of aid will depend on a diversity of resources,” she said.

world.title: Kenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national park
world.snippet: Potential toxic substance detected in several of 15 elephants found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli national park Officials are investigating th...
world.content:
Officials are investigating the deaths of 15 elephants over the past month in Kenya’s Amboseli national park.

The Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said 10 of the elephants showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days.

The remaining five carcasses were too decomposed or had been scavenged, making it impossible to establish the cause of death, the wildlife authority said.

Most of those affected were female elephants and their calves, with only one male among the dead. The deaths happened in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku ranch areas surrounding the park, officials said.

Kenya has previously recorded incidents of elephants being poisoned as a result of poaching and human-wildlife conflict.

Preliminary tests on samples collected from the elephants by a laboratory at the University of Nairobi detected a “potential toxic substance,” while separate analyses by a government laboratory were negative for the toxins tested. KWS said further tests are under way.

“Environmental investigations are also being undertaken, including the analysis of water sources and other potential environmental contaminants within the affected areas, to establish whether the elephants were exposed to a common source,” the authority said in a statement.

The authorities sought to reassure the public, saying there was no evidence the condition could be transmitted to humans.

Amboseli is world-renowned for its herds of elephants and its savannah landscapes, with Kilimanjaro visible across the border in Tanzania.

It is estimated there are about 2,000 elephants in the park.

With Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

world.title: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger
world.snippet: Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition Uganda has launched emergen...
world.content:
Uganda has launched emergency food relief distribution after at least 19 deaths from hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country.

A crisis has been building in the Karamoja region of Uganda as crops have failed without the season’s expected rains, leaving the region’s 1.5 million people facing acute food shortages and rising malnutrition.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (Fews Net), a global mapping network designed to raise the alert on food security, reported the situation had deteriorated to a crisis across Karamoja.

In the first large-scale operation of its kind organised by the Ugandan government after the funding void left by aid cuts, authorities announced plans to distribute 9,400 tonnes of relief food over the next two months. The supplies were procured using a 45bn-shilling (£9m) emergency funding allocation, approved by parliament.

Sam Engola, minister for disaster preparedness and refugees, launched the aid distribution efforts at a primary school in Lodiko sub-county in Kaabong district on Wednesday.

“The president does not want to hear of anyone in Karamoja dying of hunger. I am here to supervise the distribution of this food to the end. I will ensure that everyone receives food. No one will be left behind,” Engola said.

Karamoja is experiencing its most severe dry spell in years. Farmers have lost crops since the last meaningful rainfall was recorded in April – the beginning of the planting season.

Angelina Nakiru, a 21-year-old mother of two in Rupa, about 5 miles from Moroto town in Karamoja, said she was struggling to feed her children after all her crops failed. Now she goes early each morning to join other women at a small-scale grinding mill where machines are used to crush rock into powder to wash out gold-bearing ore. The pay is meagre.

“The work is dusty and exhausting, but it is the only way I can earn money to buy a cup of maize and beans to feed the children,” Nakiru said.

“If I don’t, the children will sleep hungry. Other days when I fail to get the meagre income from the mill, we go to bed on empty stomachs,” she said.

“The situation is terrible. People are starving and dying due to hunger. The government must come to the rescue of the people.”

Health facilities report treating hundreds of children for severe malnutrition. A nutrition report published in June found nearly half of the population in Karamoja’s Kaabong and Kotido districts in a crisis situation.

Experts attribute the region’s recurring food insecurity and vulnerability to climate crisis shocks, environmental degradation such as deforestation and overgrazing, as well as poverty and low agricultural productivity.

In 2022, a devastating hunger crisis claimed more than 2,200 lives, according to figures from Uganda’s human rights commission body.

While emergency food aid is expected to provide short-term relief, the government said it remained committed to implementing long-term remedial measures with the recently approved Karamoja regional development plan, which is intended to strengthen communities’ resilience to drought.

John Baptist Lokii, minister for Karamoja, said: “The government will provide drought-resistant, disease-resistant and early-maturing seeds ahead of the next planting season.”

Agnes Kirabo, executive director of Uganda’s Food Rights Alliance (FRA), said the government was taking the lead on distribution as a necessity as much as a policy choice as the landscape of humanitarian aid had changed dramatically.

Following significant funding cuts, most notably from USAID, which previously had an annual budget of about $42.8bn (£32.bn), agencies such as the World Food Programme (WFP) have been forced to drastically scale back their aid.

In Uganda, the WFP has phased out food assistance for 63% of the refugee population, cutting off more than 1 million people from aid, and reducing rations to just 663,000 recipients.

“This transition should not be viewed solely as a reaction to aid cuts, but also as a positive shift towards nationally owned, sustainable development. Government leadership is a constructive move, provided it is part of a long-term strategy to establish durable national systems,” said Kirabo.

“Emergency food distribution is a life-saving measure, not a permanent solution. To break this cycle, we must address the root causes of food insecurity through structural reforms.”

The FRA, Kirabo said, wanted access to food to be made a fundamental human right and the government to turn its attention to water infrastructure and climate resilience. “Karamoja possesses adequate rainfall and water routes to achieve food self-sufficiency, but requires the political will to strategically invest in water infrastructure for production,” she said.

“Ultimately, the Karamoja hunger crisis is a governance crisis. The government’s leadership in this emergency is welcome, but it must be matched by the political will to implement the systemic changes required to permanently protect the people of Karamoja and Uganda from predictable, preventable hunger.”

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report
